notes: Edition composed by Claude from the collected headlines, reading titles and metadata only.
Each narrative is an idea that joins several different events; what it joins is listed at the top. It commits to a claim, and the last rung of every narrative is the case against it. Read both.
Where a narrative continues one from the previous edition it says what has changed since; every edition is kept, so the reader can step back to where we were.

A narrative may also resume one that stopped in the last four weeks ('resumes' gives that edition's stamp and the narrative's id), and may be written from a subject the site's notebook has been keeping ('builds'); such a narrative can cite headlines from earlier days, each shown with its date, beside at least three of the day's own.

Each narrative ends with 'How we got here': four horizons, since 2020, since 2008, since 1989 and since 1945, each the start of a regime the headlines are living inside, and sometimes a fifth that reaches further back and names its own starting year. They are a trajectory, not a verdict.

Each narrative sets one or two things to watch for: what should follow, by when, if its join is right. Later editions check them against their headlines; the ledger is data/watch.json and the count stands beside the narrative's firmness.

Each narrative looks ahead: the precedent its join most resembles, two or three paths with one favoured, and where the trajectory points over a decade. That is the writer's anticipation, drawn on what it knows of history and not only on the headlines; the expectations are the earliest dated signs of the favoured path, and are how the site checks it.
The connections are made by the model, not by the publishers. Follow any headline to the original report before repeating it.
Books and trajectories appear only where they change how a fragment or a horizon reads.

readings.line: For a week, governments outside the three powers have made deals without Washington, whose tariffs hit allies as well as rivals.

watch.what: A government outside the US, China and Russia names the new US tariffs as a reason when it signs or speeds up a trade deal.
watch.because: If the week's deals are an answer to Washington rather than separate routine diplomacy, the tariff list should start appearing in the reasons governments give for them.

watch.what: Canada concludes trade talks with India, or signs a trade or investment agreement with Qatar or another Gulf state.
watch.because: Canada is both a likely target of US tariffs and a party to two of this week's talks, so if the deals are hedging it should be among the first to close one.

ahead.precedent: The closest case is 2017 to 2019. After the US left the Trans-Pacific Partnership in January 2017 and put tariffs on allies' steel in 2018, the other eleven members signed a revised pact in March 2018 and the EU and Japan signed their own agreement in July 2018. Those deals held and grew, but the US market stayed open to most of their members on old terms. This time the reported list taxes Europe and fourteen more countries at once, so there is no group of allies left outside it.

paths.name: More deals, few named reasons
paths.text: Through the first half of 2027 more bilateral and regional agreements are concluded, including India's talks with Canada and the EU's with partners in Asia and the Gulf, while most governments avoid naming Washington so as to keep talks with it open. The new tariffs take effect for most of the list. The week's mix of small steps, visas, a power link, investment talks, continues because each costs little and provokes no one.
paths.sign: Two governments that are both on the new US tariff list sign a trade or investment agreement with each other.

paths.name: Exemptions bought in Washington
paths.text: Several governments on the list buy lower rates with promises to purchase US energy, aircraft or arms, as Japan and the EU did in the summer of 2025, and slow their other talks. That would show the week's deals were a bargaining position rather than a change of direction.
paths.sign: A government on the list announces purchases of US energy, arms or aircraft alongside a tariff exemption.

paths.name: Tariffs postponed after market falls
paths.text: The fall in the Nasdaq and warnings of recession lead the White House to delay the list. This is unlikely because tariffs have been announced through earlier market falls since 2025.
paths.sign: The White House delays the new tariffs and names market conditions or ongoing talks.

ahead.decade: Over ten years the share of middle powers' trade that runs under their own agreements is likely to keep rising, and the US market becomes one large customer among several rather than the one every deal is built around.

readings.change: Since 18 November the deals have kept coming: the EU and Indonesia signed a free trade agreement on 21 November, India and Belarus agreed closer ties on 22 November, Iraq and Egypt dropped entry visas on 24 November, and today Jordan signed agreements with Uzbekistan and Qatar talked trade with Canada. What is new is the other side: Washington is reported to have tariffs ready for China, Europe and fourteen more countries.
readings.claim: Since 21 November the EU and Indonesia have signed a trade agreement, India has held talks with Canada and Belarus, Iraq and Egypt have dropped entry visas, Egypt has prepared to switch on a power link with Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Canada have discussed more trade and investment, and Jordan's king has signed agreements with Uzbekistan's president. On the day of the last two, outlets in Italy, Israel and Qatar reported that Trump has new tariffs ready for China, Europe and fourteen more countries. Read together, the deals are the slow answer and the tariffs the reason for it: governments that can no longer count on cheap access to the US market are building access to each other's, one small agreement at a time.

fragments.label: Europe and Asia
fragments.text: On 21 November Portugal's SAPO reported the EU and Indonesia signing a free trade agreement after a decade of negotiation, and India's Economic Times reported the sixth round of India-Canada trade talks concluded. On 22 November the same paper reported India and Belarus deciding to deepen ties in industry and defence. Jordan's Khaberni reported on 21 November that Jordan and the EU were strengthening their economic partnership on two tracks.

fragments.label: The Arab world and Central Asia
fragments.text: On 24 November Iraq's al-Mada reported an Iraqi-Egyptian agreement to cancel entry visas, and Arab News reported Saudi EXIM sealing five agreements at Berne Union meetings in Tokyo. Today Al-Anbat and Ammon in Jordan report King Abdullah and Uzbekistan's president witnessing an exchange of agreements and issuing a joint statement. Egypt's Masrawy reports trial operation of the electricity link with Saudi Arabia beginning next week.

fragments.label: The Americas and Britain
fragments.text: Al Jazeera Net reports Qatar and Canada discussing a wider strategic partnership with more trade and investment. Argentina's Minuto Uno reports Milei travelling to Paraguay amid what it calls a regional political reconfiguration. On 24 November Al Jazeera Net carried Andy Burnham praising a trade deal with Europe.

fragments.label: New duties by name
fragments.text: Italy's Il Messaggero reports Trump saying new tariffs on China and Europe are ready, and Israel's Walla Money says the list covers China, Europe and fourteen more countries. Al Jazeera Net reports the Nasdaq down 1.45% as the tariffs are awaited. Anadolu reports the EU itself introducing import restrictions under pressure from its hybrid carmakers.

fragments.label: What the deals share
fragments.text: None of these agreements is large on its own, and most were long in preparation. What they share is that each widens a country's access to a market other than the American one, through visas, a power link, investment talks or tariff cuts. Beside a US list that taxes allies by name, they read as insurance bought slowly by governments that expect selling to the US to cost more and cannot change that.

fragments.label: What five days show
fragments.text: One day of such headlines is ordinary diplomacy. Five days of them, from at least nine governments on three continents while a tariff list is drawn up, is a pattern that a single day hides. The EU's own import restrictions show these governments also close doors where their industries are hurt, so the movement is towards chosen partners rather than towards open trade.

fragments.label: Long talks, not new answers
fragments.text: The EU-Indonesia agreement took a decade and India and Canada are only in a sixth round, so these deals began long before any tariff list and would have been signed anyway. No headline quotes a government naming US tariffs as its reason. A state visit from Uzbekistan and a Saudi-Egyptian power link planned for years are diplomacy that any week contains.

fragments.label: Where the events part
fragments.text: The events do not share a form. EU-Indonesia is a binding treaty, Iraq-Egypt is a visa rule, Qatar-Canada is a conversation, Milei's trip is about regional politics, and the US list is a reported threat with no decree yet. A sample with many papers from Jordan, Qatar and Saudi Arabia will also over-report Arab and Gulf diplomacy, which those outlets cover every day.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: The pandemic of 2020 taught governments that one foreign supplier could stop a factory or a hospital, and the invasion of Ukraine in 2022 taught them that trade could be cut for political reasons. Washington's first answer was to bring production home and trade with friends, the policy Janet Yellen called friend-shoring in April 2022. The second Trump administration then taxed friends as well: on 2 April 2025 it announced duties on almost every trading partner, allies included, and Japan and the EU bought lower rates that summer with promises of investment and energy purchases. That removed the distinction friend-shoring rested on. The deals in these headlines, from the EU and Indonesia on 21 November to Jordan and Uzbekistan this week, are made in a world where being a US ally no longer exempts a country from US tariffs. Walla's report of a new list naming Europe and fourteen more countries shows the 2025 settlements did not close the matter.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: The 2008 crisis ended the last attempt at a single global trade round. The Doha talks broke down in Geneva in July 2008, weeks before Lehman Brothers failed, and were never revived; governments turned to deals between pairs and blocs. The United States led that turn with the Trans-Pacific Partnership and then left it in January 2017. The other eleven signatories went ahead and signed a revised pact in Santiago in March 2018, and the EU and Japan signed their own agreement that July. Britain's vote to leave the EU in 2016 added a large country in search of partners; it joined the Pacific pact in December 2024, and Andy Burnham's praise of a trade deal with Europe, carried by Al Jazeera Net on 24 November, shows the question is still argued at home. The habit this week's deals rely on, middle powers finishing agreements without waiting for Washington, was learned between 2017 and 2019.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: The end of the Cold War folded most of the world into one trading system. The World Trade Organization opened on 1 January 1995, Jordan joined it in 2000 and China in December 2001, and the five Central Asian republics, Uzbekistan among them, became independent states able to sign their own agreements in 1991. The system rested on two things: a tariff cut for one member was a cut for all, and the United States was the largest open market. Jordan's path shows the change. In 2000 it signed the first US free trade agreement with an Arab country, and for two decades its trade policy was built around American buyers. This week Al-Anbat and Ammon report its king signing agreements with Uzbekistan's president, three days after Khaberni reported closer ties with the EU. A country that once tied its trade to one partner is spreading it, which is what the WTO's decline as a place to negotiate has left most middle-sized economies to do.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: The order these deals still sit inside was built after 1945 by people who remembered the 1930s. The US Smoot-Hawley tariff of 1930 and the retaliation it drew helped cut world trade by about two thirds, and governments retreated into closed blocs such as the imperial preference Britain agreed at Ottawa in 1932. The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, signed at Geneva in 1947 by twenty-three countries, answered with one rule above the others: a tariff cut for one member must be given to all. The United States opened its market as part of the Cold War, and the dollar fixed at Bretton Woods financed the trade. Karl Polanyi argued in 1944 that markets pulled loose from society provoke a move to pull them back. The list reported by Il Messaggero and Walla charges countries different rates by name, the opposite of the 1947 rule, and the week's bilateral deals are how others recover part of what that rule used to give them.

readings.line: A US firm's treatment by regulators now depends partly on its closeness to the president, who has money in some of them.

watch.what: A US agency closes, settles or narrows its investigation of Nvidia with no charge against the company or its chief.
watch.because: If treatment follows closeness to the president, the investigation should end gently soon after he and the attorney general publicly backed the firm; ordinary enforcement would run on.

watch.what: Reports of Huang's 1 December congressional hearing say lawmakers asked about Trump's personal gain from Nvidia's shares.
watch.because: If the president's own money is part of the story, his opponents should raise it at the first public hearing rather than ask only about chips reaching China.

ahead.precedent: The closest case is Teapot Dome. In 1921 and 1922 Interior Secretary Albert Fall leased naval oil reserves in Wyoming and California to Harry Sinclair and Edward Doheny without competitive bidding and took about $400,000 from them; a Senate inquiry exposed it, and in 1929 Fall became the first cabinet member convicted for crimes in office. The present differs in that the favours reported run through agencies answering to the president, and the gain described is to the president's own holdings, which the main federal conflict-of-interest law does not cover.

paths.name: Hearings, not penalties
paths.text: From January the new Congress holds hearings on Nvidia, the GEO jail sale and the OakNorth charter, but the agencies close or narrow their own cases and no firm close to the president faces a large fine in 2027. The week points this way because the attorney general has already given Nvidia a public character reference while the investigation is open.
paths.sign: A US agency closes or narrows its Nvidia investigation without charges.

paths.name: Huawei verdict becomes a bargaining chip
paths.text: Huawei's sentencing or penalties are delayed or softened as part of tariff talks with China, as Trump said in May 2019 that Huawei could be included in a trade deal. That would confirm that outcomes for foreign firms are also set by the president's interests rather than by the verdict.
paths.sign: A report links Huawei's sentencing or penalties to US-China trade talks.

paths.name: An inspector reverses a favour
paths.text: An inspector general or federal judge finds the GEO price or the OakNorth charter improper and it is reversed. Unlikely within a year, because such reviews are slow and the agencies involved are led by the president's appointees.
paths.sign: An inspector general opens a review of the GEO jail purchase or the OakNorth charter.

ahead.decade: Over the decade the likely result is a law, passed after this administration, that extends conflict-of-interest rules to a president's holdings, as Watergate produced the 1978 Ethics in Government Act; until then closeness to the president will keep showing in outcomes.

readings.change: Yesterday's narrative had Nvidia's chief returning with the president's support while penalties fell on firms abroad. Today the US attorney general called Nvidia a good corporate citizen while saying little about the investigation, outlets put a figure on what Trump gains from Huang's return, and a US jury convicted Huawei. The pattern now reaches beyond chips, to a bank charter, a jail sale and a medal.
readings.claim: Outlets in France, New Zealand and Greece reported on what Trump stands to gain from Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia, while Korea's Hankyoreh quoted the US attorney general calling Nvidia a good corporate citizen and saying little about the investigation into it. In the same day's news a Kushner-backed bank won a US charter, GEO was reported to have sold the administration a jail for $453 million after valuing it at $67 million, Trump announced the Medal of Freedom for Giuliani, and a US jury convicted Huawei of trade secret theft and fraud. The joining fact is one actor: the federal government's decisions about firms and people line up with their closeness to the president. In Nvidia's case the outlets describe the president's own gain, which turns an investigation of the firm into a decision that touches his money.

events.label: Trump's gain from Huang's return
Attorney general praises Nvidia during probe
US jury convicts Huawei
Kushner-backed bank wins US charter

fragments.label: What the president gains
fragments.text: franceinfo asks whether Trump got richer from Huang's surprise return to the head of Nvidia, and the NZ Herald estimates how much he stands to make. Greece's EfSyn carries a CNN analysis of Trump's big risk and of concern among Republicans. Fortune reports that Huang confessed to more affairs and the board took him back anyway.

fragments.label: What the attorney general said
fragments.text: Korea's Hankyoreh reports the US attorney general declining to say much about the Nvidia investigation beyond calling the company a good corporate citizen. That is a character reference from the official in charge of the prosecutors, given while the case is open.

rungs.label: A bank, a jail, a medal, a verdict

fragments.label: Decisions at home
fragments.text: CNBC reports that OakNorth, backed by Jared Kushner, has secured a US bank charter. IBT UK reports that GEO valued an immigration jail at $67 million before selling it to the administration for $453 million. Canada's Niagara Falls Review reports that Trump will give the Medal of Freedom to Giuliani, described as a fierce political ally.

fragments.label: A foreign rival in court
fragments.text: WELT and Handelsblatt in Germany, La Tercera in Chile and the BBC report a US jury finding Huawei guilty after lengthy proceedings. The German and Chilean versions stress money laundering and bank fraud; the BBC reports guilt for stealing trade secrets and acquittal on racketeering.

fragments.label: Closeness decides the tone
fragments.text: The joining actor is the federal government under one president. Where a firm or person is close to him, the reported outcomes are soft: praise for Nvidia from the attorney general, a charter for a bank tied to his son-in-law, a price for a jail nearly seven times its earlier valuation, a medal for an ally. Where the firm is a foreign rival, the outcome is a jury verdict.

fragments.label: When the president holds the stake
fragments.text: Favour for allies is old in Washington. The new element is that the outlets in France and New Zealand are writing about the president's own gain from a firm his attorney general is investigating, so an enforcement decision is also a decision about his money.

fragments.label: Different institutions decided
fragments.text: The Huawei case was brought by prosecutors years ago and decided by a jury, which acquitted on racketeering; it shows something about US courts, not about the president's favour. A bank charter comes from a regulator after a long application, and CNBC frames OakNorth as part of a wider push by foreign digital banks. A medal is an honour, not a regulatory act, and the GEO price may reflect contract terms the headline does not give.

fragments.label: Where the events part
fragments.text: The events share an actor but not a mechanism: one is a criminal verdict, one a licence, one a purchase, one an honour and one a remark about an open case. Closeness to a president can be found after the fact for almost any large firm, and no headline shows a decision that went against the evidence before it.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: ChatGPT's release in November 2022 turned Nvidia's chips into the scarce input of a new industry. The company's market value passed a trillion dollars in May 2023 and kept rising, so that by these headlines Huang's return moves Korea's main index and a fall in Nvidia shares moves Wall Street. In the same years Washington made the chips an instrument of policy: export controls on advanced chips to China in October 2022 and October 2023 meant that what Nvidia could sell, and to whom, was settled in the Commerce Department. A firm whose sales depend on government licences, and whose share price sits in millions of retirement accounts, is a firm whose relations with the White House matter to both sides. That is the setting for franceinfo and the NZ Herald asking what Trump gains from Huang's return, and for the attorney general's choice, reported by Hankyoreh, to praise the company rather than discuss the case against it.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: In September 2008 the US government let Lehman Brothers fail and two days later rescued AIG. Congress passed a $700 billion rescue fund in October, and for the first time in decades Washington decided, firm by firm, which large companies would survive. Adam Tooze's account of the decade shows how that crisis made the relation between governments and particular firms a lasting political question rather than an emergency measure. One effect shows in the CNBC headline about OakNorth: after 2008 regulators granted very few new bank charters, so winning one became a sign of official acceptance as much as a licence to lend. OakNorth's charter, with Jared Kushner's backing, comes as foreign digital banks push into the US market. The same period made the federal government a large buyer of private services, including detention, which is the background to GEO, a private prison operator, selling a jail to the administration at a large gain.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: Huawei was founded in Shenzhen in 1987 and grew with the opening that followed China's entry to the WTO in 2001, selling network equipment across Africa, Europe and Latin America at prices Western firms could not match. Its conflict with US law began as commercial: Cisco sued it in 2003 over copied router software and settled in 2004. Washington then recast the dispute as one of security. In December 2018 Canada arrested Huawei's finance chief, Meng Wanzhou, on a US warrant, and federal prosecutors in New York later charged the company with bank fraud, trade secret theft and racketeering. By these headlines a jury has now convicted on theft and fraud but not racketeering. The years after 1989 made Chinese firms direct competitors of American ones in the same markets, which is why outlets in Germany, Chile and Britain read a verdict against a foreign firm beside leniency towards a domestic one.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: After 1945 the American state paid for most of the technology that mattered. The workshop that named artificial intelligence at Dartmouth in 1956 was foundation-funded, and after Sputnik in 1957 the Pentagon set up the research agency that later built the internet. Firms built what the state commissioned, and the rules for that relation were written for contractors and officials. After Watergate the Ethics in Government Act of 1978 required senior officials to disclose their finances, but the federal criminal conflict-of-interest statute has never applied to the president, a gap covered for decades by the custom of blind trusts. Seventy years after Dartmouth the builder of the decisive technology is a private company, and the headlines from France and New Zealand about Trump's gains from Nvidia describe a president with a stake in a firm his own administration is investigating. The postwar rules dealt with officials who bought from firms, not with a president who holds shares in them.

readings.line: Drones now reach far behind any front, so civilian buildings and roads in countries at peace are being prepared for strikes.

watch.what: A European government outside Ukraine announces money or a rule for shelters in hospitals, schools or new housing and names drones as the reason.
watch.because: If range is the common cause, the planning NRK describes for hospitals should turn into civilian rules in a country not at war, not only into defence spending.

watch.what: A Gulf government orders new protection, evacuation drills or access limits for high-rise office towers after the Riyadh attacks.
watch.because: If strikes are now aimed at office districts rather than oil plants, the answer should move into the buildings themselves, as it is in Norway and Finland.

ahead.precedent: The closest case is the Cold War in Sweden and Switzerland. From the late 1950s Sweden dispersed its air force to road strips, and from 1963 Swiss law required a shelter place for every resident; both were built against an attack that never came, and both were run down after 1991. The present differs in that the strikes are already landing, Riyadh's tallest tower twice in one week, and the weapon costs far less than the defence against it.

paths.name: Shelters written into building rules
paths.text: Through 2027 the Nordic and Baltic states and Poland add protection requirements for hospitals and new public buildings and fund more reserve road strips, while Gulf states add hardening and drills for office towers. The week points this way because the preparations come from health and interior ministries as well as defence ones, which is how a measure becomes part of a building code.
paths.sign: A government publishes a shelter or protection requirement for new hospitals or public buildings, naming drones.

paths.name: Money goes to interceptors instead
paths.text: Governments put the money into cheaper interceptors, like the missile unian says Ukraine has built for a new air defence system, and leave buildings as they are. That is quicker and more visible, and could stall the civilian measures for several years.
paths.sign: A European government announces a large counter-drone or interceptor purchase while delaying a civil defence plan.

paths.name: Ceasefires take the urgency away
paths.text: If the Russia and Iran wars both reach ceasefires by spring, shelter and dispersal plans are shelved as they were after 1991. Unlikely in that time, because strikes on Riyadh and on Ukraine's towns continued through this month's talks.
paths.sign: A government delays or cuts a civil defence budget, citing a ceasefire.

ahead.decade: Within ten years protection against strikes is likely to be a normal part of building codes and hospital standards across northern Europe and the Gulf, paid for from civilian budgets rather than defence ones.

readings.claim: Norway's NRK reports that hospitals now need bomb shelters as drone warfare spreads, Iraq's defence minister has ordered military units out of cities, French and Dutch jets have practised landing on a Finnish motorway, and Finland's interior minister says its public hazard warning test went better this time. In the same days a Houthi attack hit the tallest tower in Riyadh's financial district for the second time in a week, a drone entered Polish airspace, and Ukraine published another day's power cut schedules after Russian strikes. The joining cause is range: cheap drones and missiles now reach offices, grids and towns hundreds of kilometres from any fighting. Governments are answering by moving defence into the places people live and work, and by moving soldiers out of them.

events.label: Hospitals and public warnings prepared
Iraq moves military units out of cities
Jets practise landing on Finnish motorway
Riyadh tower hit twice in a week
Drone enters Polish airspace
Ukraine's towns under strike and outage

fragments.label: Riyadh and Poland
fragments.text: Arab News reports 11 people injured after a Houthi attack on a tower in Riyadh's financial district, and Walla reports the same attack. Taiwan's UDN reports that the Saudi capital's tallest skyscraper has been hit twice in one week. Handelsblatt reports a drone entering Polish airspace.

fragments.label: Ukraine's towns
fragments.text: unian publishes the power outage schedules for 25 November, and Lenta reports Zelensky complaining of major problems in the regions after Russian strikes. unian also reports that Ukraine has built a missile for a new air defence system meant to shoot down drones.

fragments.label: Hospitals, warnings, barracks
fragments.text: Norway's NRK reports that as drone warfare spreads worldwide, hospitals need bomb shelters. Yle reports Finland's interior minister saying the public hazard information test succeeded better this time. Iraq's al-Mada reports new directives from the defence minister to evacuate military units from cities.

fragments.label: Roads as runways
fragments.text: France's La Dépêche reports Rafale jets training to land on a national road in Finland. Vietnam's An ninh Thủ đô reports a Dutch F-35 landing on a Finnish motorway as NATO tests a plan for its aircraft to survive a strike on their bases.

fragments.label: Two answers to one cause
fragments.text: The common cause is range. When a drone can reach an office tower or a power station hundreds of kilometres from a front, defence stops being something done at a border. Governments answer in two directions at once: they harden civilian places, with shelters under hospitals and warning tests, and they move military targets away from people, by sending jets to roads or units out of cities. Both bring the civilian landscape into military planning, in countries at war and at peace.

fragments.label: Most of this is old
fragments.text: Sweden and Finland practised road landings throughout the Cold War, Finland has built shelters under its cities for decades, and Riyadh has been under Houthi fire since 2015. NRK's piece is a feature, not a policy, and Iraq's order comes in the same week Baghdad moves to take over Kurdish oilfields, which may be its real reason.

fragments.label: Where the events part
fragments.text: The Riyadh tower, Ukraine's towns and the Polish incursion are attacks; the Norwegian and Finnish items are planning and drills; the Iraqi order is an administrative step with no stated cause. Grouping a war's targets with a peacetime exercise may make ordinary readiness look like a new trend.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: The war over Nagorno-Karabakh in autumn 2020 showed that Turkish and Israeli drones could decide a war in forty-four days, and defence ministries rewrote their plans. Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 turned the lesson against cities: from October 2022 Russian missiles and Iranian-designed Shahed drones struck Ukraine's power stations, which is why unian still publishes daily outage schedules. Ukraine answered with drones reaching refineries and airfields deep in Russia, and on 1 June 2025 it launched them from lorries against bombers thousands of kilometres from the front. In the Gulf the Houthis kept up strikes on Saudi Arabia, and by these headlines they have now hit Riyadh's tallest tower twice in one week. The change in this decade is that strikes no longer stop at a front line, so the distance a country keeps from a war no longer tells it how safe its hospitals are, the point NRK makes from Norway.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: The Houthi movement took Sanaa in September 2014, and a Saudi-led coalition went to war against it in March 2015. Unable to match Saudi air power, the Houthis acquired and built cheap missiles and drones and aimed them at Saudi cities, airports and oil sites. On 14 September 2019 drones and missiles hit the Abqaiq processing plant and halved Saudi oil output for several days, the first time a cheap weapon reached one of the most expensive targets in the world economy. Grégoire Chamayou argued in 2013 that the drone changes war by letting one side strike without being exposed; the Houthi campaign shows that a side with little money can use the same advantage against a rich state. The coalition statements reported from Lebanon and Saudi Arabia promise a firm response, as they have since 2015, while the attacks on Riyadh's financial district show the target moving from oil plants to office towers.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: After 1991 European governments cut what they had kept for a war at home. Sweden closed most of the road bases its air force had used since the 1950s, and civil defence budgets across NATO shrank. At the same time the means of long-range strike spread beyond states. On 1 May 2000 Washington switched off the deliberate error in civilian GPS, and cheap navigation made small drones possible for almost anyone. In October 2001 the United States made the first armed Predator strike in Afghanistan, and the drone became a weapon. Mary Kaldor described the wars of the period as wars without fronts, fought among civilians. The French and Dutch jets landing on a Finnish motorway, reported by La Dépêche and An ninh Thủ đô, are practising what Sweden largely dropped after 1991: keeping aircraft away from bases an enemy can locate. What has changed is that the threat is a weapon a militia can afford.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.lens: LAWS OF WAR / CIVIL DEFENCE / AIR POWER
horizons.text: The rules on how strikes may touch civilians were written after the bombing of Dresden, Tokyo and Hiroshima. The Geneva Conventions of 1949 protected hospitals, and Additional Protocol I of 1977 went further: article 54 protects what civilians need to survive, and article 58 asks states to avoid placing military objectives within or near densely populated areas. The Iraqi defence minister's order to move military units out of cities, reported by al-Mada, is article 58 in practice, whatever its immediate motive. The Cold War added civil defence: Switzerland required a shelter place for every resident from the 1960s, and Finland built shelters under its cities. In June 1982 Israel used drones over the Bekaa Valley to locate and blind Syria's air defences, the beginning of the drone as a weapon of war. The Norwegian hospitals that NRK says need shelters are protected by the 1949 rules and within reach of the weapon first proved in 1982.

readings.line: States spy on and sabotage each other through private firms, and governments now leave the firms to defend themselves.

watch.what: A European government publicly names a Russian, Iranian or Chinese service as behind an attack on a named private company.
watch.because: If states are now pursuing each other through firms, the attributions that follow should name companies as the victims, not only ministries or agencies.

watch.what: Finland's security police or prosecutors name a suspect or a foreign state in the Laukaa gunpowder factory espionage case.
watch.because: If the Laukaa case belongs to the same pattern as the ships and the airline, it should turn out to involve a foreign service rather than an ordinary crime.

ahead.precedent: On 30 July 1916 German agents blew up the Black Tom munitions depot in New York harbour while the United States was still neutral, because the shells were bound for Britain and France; a shell plant at Kingsland, New Jersey, burned in January 1917. A claims commission found Germany liable only in 1939. The present differs in that most attacks now come from abroad over networks, the targets include shipping software and an AI laboratory, and governments answer with advice to firms rather than with war.

paths.name: Security costs moved onto firms
paths.text: Over the next year Britain, Finland and other European governments set binding security and reporting duties for firms in defence supply, shipping and energy, and Washington tightens rules for AI labs, while attributions to named states stay rare. The week points this way because the official response in each case is advice to the target or an investigation, not action against the attacker.
paths.sign: A government orders firms in a named sector to meet new security or reporting rules, citing sabotage or espionage.

paths.name: Named attribution and expulsions
paths.text: A European government names a Russian or Iranian service for an attack on a firm and expels diplomats, as Britain and its allies did after the Salisbury poisoning in March 2018. Possible because Britain and Finland have attributed attacks before, but the evidence usually takes months.
paths.sign: A European government expels diplomats after attributing an attack on a company.

paths.name: A truce on sabotage in talks
paths.text: The Ukraine or Iran talks include commitments to stop attacks on civilian companies and ships. Unlikely because no reported draft covers sabotage, and neither side admits to carrying it out.
paths.sign: A reported draft in the Ukraine or Iran talks includes a clause on cyberattacks or sabotage against companies.

ahead.decade: Over the decade firms in defence supply, shipping, energy and AI are likely to carry security duties close to those of state agencies, with vetting, reporting and insurance costs that their smaller suppliers will struggle to meet.

readings.claim: NPR reports the US government investigating Iranian ties to as many as 50 hacked commercial vessels, Israel's Walla describes Iranians using AI in an attempt to attack an airline flying to Israel, Finnish media report suspected espionage at the Laukaa gunpowder factory, and the BBC reports British businesses that support Ukraine being told to act now against Russian sabotage. In the same news a US judge freed a Saudi engineer accused of listening in on OpenAI meetings, BBC Verify traced a China-linked network smearing Taiwanese candidates with AI fakes, and the CIA and the US intelligence director's office reported a breach, after one at the FBI. The shared mechanism is that states pursue their contests through private targets, shipowners, an airline, a munitions plant, suppliers and an AI lab. The public response is to tell those targets to protect themselves, while the agencies that would protect them are breached as well.

events.label: CIA and intelligence office breached
Iran-linked attacks on ships and an airline
Suspected espionage at Finnish gunpowder plant
British firms told to guard against sabotage
Engineer accused of spying on OpenAI freed
AI fakes against Taiwan candidates

fragments.label: Ships, an airline, a factory
fragments.text: NPR reports the US government investigating Iranian ties to as many as 50 hacked commercial vessels. Walla's technology section describes how Iranians tried to use AI to attack an airline flying to Israel. Finland's Länsi-Savo, citing Yle, reports suspected espionage at the gunpowder factory in Laukaa.

fragments.label: Suppliers and a laboratory
fragments.text: The BBC reports businesses supporting Ukraine being told to act now to protect themselves against Russian sabotage. Al Jazeera Net reports a US judge ordering the release of a Saudi engineer accused of eavesdropping on OpenAI meetings.

fragments.label: Breaches and fakes
fragments.text: Portugal's SAPO, Russia's Kommersant citing the New York Times, and El País report a cyberattack on an unclassified CIA system and on the office of the director of national intelligence. Argentina's Clarín frames it as concern growing in the United States after the attack on the FBI. BBC Verify reports a China-linked network using AI fakes to smear candidates in Taiwan's elections.

fragments.label: The target carries the burden
fragments.text: In each case a foreign state, by the headlines' own attributions, pursues its contest with other states by reaching private bodies: shipowners, an airline, an ammunition plant, suppliers to Ukraine, an AI lab, candidates' reputations. The public response reported is advice and investigation: British firms are told to act, and the US investigates after the ships are already hacked. Meanwhile the intelligence agencies that would warn those firms report breaches of their own, so the practical defence falls to the targets.

fragments.label: Old practice, weak cases
fragments.text: Industrial espionage and sabotage are as old as industry; German agents blew up a New Jersey munitions depot in 1916. The ship hacks may be criminal ransomware with an Iranian link rather than a state operation, the Saudi engineer was released and is only accused, and the Laukaa case is a suspicion. The CIA breach touched an unclassified system and is state against state, not against a firm.

fragments.label: Where the events part
fragments.text: What these share is a hostile foreign hand. What they do not share is a kind of target or a method: the Taiwan fakes aim at voters, the airline story is a feature about a failed attempt, the factory case may involve a person on site, and the ships are a network attack. Three of the strongest items come from countries at war with Iran or Russia, whose press reports such attacks more readily.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: This decade's attacks on private infrastructure showed governments how much of national security sits in company hands. In December 2020 the SolarWinds breach, attributed by Washington to Russian intelligence, entered US government departments through a private software supplier. In May 2021 a ransomware attack shut Colonial Pipeline, which carries much of the fuel for the US east coast. On 24 February 2022, the day of the invasion, a hack of the Viasat satellite network cut modems across Europe. Since 2024 European governments have accused Russia of arson and sabotage against firms supplying Ukraine. The BBC's report that such businesses are told to act now comes at the end of this sequence: the state has identified the firms as targets and handed them much of the work of defending themselves. The breach at the CIA and the intelligence director's office, following one at the FBI, shows the agencies that would otherwise help under the same pressure.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: The idea that code could do physical damage became public in 2010, when Stuxnet, later attributed to the United States and Israel, was found to have wrecked centrifuges at Iran's Natanz plant. Iran's reply reached a company rather than a state: in August 2012 the Shamoon malware wiped some thirty thousand computers at Saudi Aramco. In June 2017 NotPetya, attributed to Russian military intelligence, spread from a Ukrainian accounting program to Maersk, the world's largest container line, and to Merck and others, costing billions. The pattern since 2010 is that states strike each other through companies and that attribution comes months or years later, if at all. NPR's report of a US investigation into Iranian ties to as many as fifty hacked commercial vessels follows the same route: shipping is where both the Iran war and the Ukraine war meet the world economy, and the ships belong to private owners.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: When the Cold War ended, intelligence services that had watched armies turned towards economies. The US Economic Espionage Act of 1996 made theft of trade secrets for a foreign government a federal crime, an admission that the contest between states had moved into companies. Netscape's listing in August 1995 began the commercial internet, and with it the move of a society's information from state archives to company servers. Shoshana Zuboff describes the business that followed as one built on watching users; for foreign services it meant the most valuable information now sat in firms. The OpenAI case reported by Al Jazeera Net, a Saudi engineer accused of listening in on the laboratory's meetings and then released by a US judge, belongs to this line: the most sought-after technical secrets of the decade are held by a private lab, and their first defence is its own security staff.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: The model of a state secret held partly in private hands began with the Manhattan Project. The bomb tested in New Mexico in July 1945 was built by the army with firms such as DuPont, and Klaus Fuchs, a physicist at Los Alamos, passed its design to the Soviet Union; he was convicted in Britain in 1950. The Cold War answer was vetting: security clearances for contractors' staff and secrecy rules that bound firms working on defence. Finland's gunpowder plant at Laukaa, where Yle reports suspected espionage, is the kind of site that system was built to protect, a factory supplying ammunition that European armies now need in quantity. What has changed is how many private sites now hold something another state wants: munitions makers, shipping lines, airlines and software firms are all reported as targets in a single day's headlines, far more than the vetting system was designed to cover.
